participants.cot: This respondent sees getting ahead as resting on legitimate effort and merit — hard work is very important and a good education fairly important — while dismissing improper or unearned routes: political connections and race or ethnicity are not important at all, and coming from a wealthy family is not very important. Giving bribes belongs to that same category of under-the-table shortcuts rather than merit, so the same outlook points to rating it as not important at all. His high religious participation supports a moral rejection of corrupt payments, and his general trust that people can usually be trusted fits a view of society — reinforced by New Zealand's low-corruption environment — where advancement does not depend on bribery. Therefore, the answer is 5.

participants.cot: Believing that poverty causes health problems and that rich people have much easier access to care, this respondent plausibly sees broader public funding as a way to narrow that gap. Their great deal of confidence in the health care system, together with rejecting the idea that doctors are mainly profit-driven or that the system is inefficient, suggests they would trust extra money to translate into real improvements rather than being wasted. That combination supports willingness to pay higher taxes for health care. At the same time, coming from a lower-income household makes the personal cost of a tax increase more tangible, which fits a fairly willing rather than fully enthusiastic response. Therefore, the answer is 2.

participants.cot: This respondent has very little confidence in the health care system, sees it as very unfair and strongly inefficient, and strongly agrees that doctors care more about their earnings than their patients. From that perspective, handing more tax money to the system seems like rewarding waste and self-interested providers rather than improving care. Her right-wing orientation and lower income position reinforce reluctance about higher taxes, and her strong disagreement that poverty causes health problems, along with opposing publicly funded care for non-citizens, suggests she does not see expanded public spending as the route to better health. Together these views point to being very unwilling to pay higher taxes for health care. Therefore, the answer is 5.
